old: she couldn't help wondering how coldly or civilly that lady would treat her now.
new: she couldn't help feeling how very unwelcome her appearance at Pemberley must be to Miss Bingley, and was curious to see how much civility that lady would show in renewing their acquaintance.
source: she could not help feeling how very unwelcome her appearance at Pemberley must be to her, and was curious to know with how much civility on that lady's side the acquaintance would now be renewed.
reason: The candidate drops Elizabeth's awareness that her visit must be very unwelcome to Miss Bingley, and turns her curiosity about the degree of civility into 'coldly or civilly', which the source doesn't say.

old: a resolution all the more necessary because she could see that every eye in the room was watching his behavior.
new: a resolution all the more necessary to make, though perhaps not the easier to keep, because she could see that the whole party's suspicions had been aroused about the two of them, and that there was scarcely an eye that did not watch his behavior when he first came into the room.
source: a resolution the more necessary to be made, but perhaps not the more easily kept, because she saw that the suspicions of the whole party were awakened against them, and that there was scarcely an eye which did not watch his behaviour when he first came into the room.
reason: The candidate drops the ironic 'but perhaps not the more easily kept' and the key point that everyone's suspicions about Darcy and Elizabeth had been aroused. It also turns 'scarcely an eye' into 'every eye'.

old: whenever she spoke to either Darcy or his sister
new: whenever she spoke to either of them
source: in spite of the smiles which overspread her face whenever she spoke to one of its objects
reason: The 'objects' of Miss Bingley's curiosity are Darcy and Elizabeth, the pair being watched, not Darcy and Georgiana. The candidate changes who she smiles at.

old: because of his very hope that those connections might one day become his own.
new: because of the very wish Elizabeth had long ago attributed to him: that they might one day become his sister's own.
source: from that very wish which Elizabeth had long ago attributed to him, of their becoming hereafter her own.
reason: 'Her own' means Georgiana's: Darcy hoped his sister would marry into the Bingley family. The candidate says Darcy wanted the connections for himself, and it drops 'which Elizabeth had long ago attributed to him'.

old: sharp, shrewd look
new: sharp, shrewish look
source: They have a sharp, shrewish look
reason: 'Shrewish' means bad-tempered and scolding. 'Shrewd' means clever, which is close to a compliment and blunts Miss Bingley's spite.

old: But on the third day her patience was rewarded by the arrival of two letters at once
new: But on the third day her complaining was over and her sister was vindicated by the arrival of two letters at once
source: but on the third her repining was over, and her sister justified, by the receipt of two letters from her at once
reason: Elizabeth had been fretting, not waiting patiently, and the letters clear Jane of neglect. The candidate turns the fretting into 'patience' and drops 'her sister justified'.

old: and sent the first one back to Epsom
new: and dismissed the one that had brought them from Epsom
source: and dismissed the chaise that brought them from Epsom.
reason: The source says only that the chaise that brought them from Epsom was dismissed. Sending it back to Epsom is invented; Epsom is where it came from.

old: checking at every turnpike and inn along the way
new: anxiously repeating them at all the turnpikes and at the inns in Barnet and Hatfield
source: anxiously renewing them at all the turnpikes, and at the inns in Barnet and Hatfield
reason: The candidate drops the place names Barnet and Hatfield. Elizabeth refers back to 'the Barnet road' in 47.5.

old: Poor Kitty is furious at having been sworn to secrecy about their attachment, but since it was told in confidence, one can't blame her.
new: Poor Kitty has been scolded for having concealed their attachment; but since it was told her in confidence, one can't wonder at it.
source: Poor Kitty has anger for having concealed their attachment; but as it was a matter of confidence, one cannot wonder.
reason: The anger is aimed at Kitty for hiding the attachment; 47.40 refers to 'the anger which she had herself incurred'. The candidate makes Kitty the angry one and invents 'sworn to secrecy'.

old: My father has gone to London with Colonel Forster
new: My father is going to London with Colonel Forster at once
source: My father is going to London with Colonel Forster instantly, to try to discover her.
reason: Jane writes that her father is about to leave, not that he has already gone. The candidate changes the timeline.

old: But self-pity, though it intruded, couldn't dominate.
new: But thoughts of herself, though they would intrude, couldn't absorb her.
source: But self, though it would intrude, could not engross her.
reason: 'Self' here means Elizabeth's own concerns (what she has just realized about Darcy). Calling it 'self-pity' adds a judgment the source doesn't make.

old: and—with only one serious, lingering look—left the room.
new: and, leaving his compliments for her relations, with only one serious parting look, went away.
source: and, leaving his compliments for her relations, with only one serious parting look, went away.
reason: The candidate drops Darcy leaving his compliments for her relations, a telling courtesy toward the Gardiners. 'Lingering' is also added.

old: might reasonably lead her to try the less dramatic approach
new: might perhaps entitle her to try the other, less interesting kind of attachment
source: that its ill success might, perhaps, authorize her to seek the other less interesting mode of attachment
reason: The narrator's ironic defense is hedged ('perhaps') and wry ('less interesting'). 'Reasonably' drops the hedge, and 'less dramatic approach' flattens the joke.

old: repeated her aunt as she ran to her room to pack.
new: repeated her aunt, as Elizabeth ran to her room to get ready.
source: repeated the other, as she ran into her room to prepare.
reason: Elizabeth is the one who runs off; Mrs. Gardiner then speaks of 'her' in the third person. The candidate's 'she' reads as the aunt.

old: "I do, indeed," said Mrs. Gardiner. "I'm coming around to your uncle's view.
new: "Upon my word," said Mrs. Gardiner, "I'm beginning to come around to your uncle's view.
source: "Upon my word," said Mrs. Gardiner, "I begin to be of your uncle's opinion.
reason: Elizabeth's question was put to her uncle. 'I do, indeed' has Mrs. Gardiner answer it with a firm belief the source doesn't give her. She is only beginning to agree.

old: for the last year or more,
new: for the last six months—no, for a whole year—
source: and for the last half year, nay, for a twelvemonth, she has been given up to nothing but amusement and vanity.
reason: The candidate loses Elizabeth's self-correction, which shows her agitation as she speaks and is not the same as 'a year or more'.

old: he's been dishonest in every sense of the word
new: he's been dissolute in every sense of the word
source: We both know that he has been profligate in every sense of the word
reason: 'Profligate' means dissolute and wasteful: sexual misconduct and spending, which is why the charge matters here. 'Dishonest' changes the charge and repeats the next clause.

old: but when questioned, Denny
new: but when questioned by him, Denny
source: Yes; but when questioned by _him_, Denny denied knowing anything of their plan
reason: The emphasis contrasts what Denny let slip to others with what he told the Colonel. Without 'by him', the reason for Jane's hope is lost.

old: with obvious triumph
new: with a very natural triumph
source: Kitty then owned, with a very natural triumph on knowing more than the rest of us
reason: Jane charitably calls Kitty's triumph 'very natural'. 'Obvious' removes the excuse she makes for Kitty and flattens Jane's voice.

old: "I don't know; I hope not.
new: "I don't know; I hope there was.
source: "I do not know: I hope there was.
reason: Elizabeth asks whether any servant did NOT know the story. Jane hopes there was one. The candidate's 'I hope not' reverses her meaning.
lead_note: Defect accepted; source wording used, since "I hope so" leaves the referent unclear.

old: nothing, therefore, could be accurately guessed on that subject. Though Elizabeth
new: nothing, therefore, could fairly be inferred from them, though Elizabeth
source: nothing, therefore, could be fairly conjectured from _that_,--though Elizabeth, who was by this time tolerably well acquainted with her own feelings, was perfectly aware
reason: The candidate breaks the sentence and leaves 'Though Elizabeth ... was perfectly aware ...' as a fragment. 'On that subject' also blurs the point: nothing could be read into her low spirits.
lead_note: Defect accepted; a comma replaces the dash because an em-dash parenthesis follows straight after.

old: said Kitty, hurt.
new: said Kitty peevishly.
source: said Kitty, fretfully.
reason: Kitty is fretful (peevish, irritable), as in 47.40. 'Hurt' makes her more sympathetic than Austen does.

old: I wouldn't trust you within fifty miles of it!
new: I wouldn't trust you as near to it as Eastbourne—not for fifty pounds!
source: I would not trust you so near it as Eastbourne, for fifty pounds!
reason: The candidate drops Eastbourne (a nearby resort that is still at a safe distance) and changes 'for fifty pounds' (not even for a large sum) into a distance. Mr. Bennet's joke is altered.
lead_note: Defect accepted; "not for fifty pounds" makes it clear to a modern reader that this is a sum refused, not a distance.

old: they were about to look for him upstairs when
new: they were about to look for him upstairs with their mother when
source: they were on the point of seeking him upstairs with their mother
reason: The candidate drops where they expected to find him.

old: there will be some money remaining
new: there will be a little money remaining
source: there will be some little money, even when all his debts are discharged, to settle on my niece
reason: Gardiner deliberately plays the sum down as 'some little money'. The size of the settlement is what the Bennets go on to puzzle over.

old: proof, I want to believe,
new: proof, I will believe,
source: His consenting to marry her is a proof, I will believe, that he is come to a right way of thinking.
reason: Jane chooses to believe it. 'I want to believe' adds doubt that isn't in the source and is out of character for Jane.
